label: Forms of cell-aggregates are shaped chiefly by surface tension toward minimal areas
claim: The forms of cells in contact with one another, and ultimately of tissues, are determined especially by surface tension, which shows itself in the production of surfaces of (relatively) minimal area.
quote: we shall probably find, and we may at least begin by assuming, that the agency of surface tension is especially manifest and important. The effect of this surface tension will chiefly manifest itself in the production of surfaces _minimae areae_
scope: cell-aggregates and tissues of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: total interface area relative to minimal configurations
candidate_data: Segmented 2D and 3D tissue images (e.g. Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Explorer) combined with published cortical-tension and laser-ablation measurements of cell interfaces.

section: Three surfaces in contact and Sachs’s Rule
label: Right-angled cell walls arise because older walls solidify before new partitions form
claim: Plant cell walls often meet at right angles (Sachs’s Rule) because an earlier wall has usually become solid and rigid before a later partition joins it, so the fluid partition sets itself at equal angles, i.e. perpendicular, to the rigid wall.
quote: such validity as the rule possesses is due to the fact that among plant-tissues it very frequently happens that one cell-wall has become solid and rigid before another and later partition-wall is developed in connection with it.
scope: plant tissues with rigid cell walls
measurable_quantities: angle at which new partitions meet existing walls
rigidity of parent wall at time of division
candidate_data: Time-lapse confocal imaging of plant meristems and segmented plant tissue datasets (e.g. published Arabidopsis shoot-apex segmentations on public repositories) giving junction angles of new versus old walls.

label: Shape of paired cells depends on relative tensions at outer surface and partition
claim: Whether two adjacent cells in a filament (as in Nostoc and its allies) are separated by flat partitions, are hemispherical, or are each more than a hemisphere depends on the relative magnitudes of the tension at the outer cell surface and at the boundary between the cells.
quote: These various conditions depend, according to what we have already learned, upon the relative magnitudes of the tensions at the surface of the cells and at the boundary between them
scope: pairs and chains of cells in filamentous lower algae and other two-celled aggregates
measurable_quantities: partition diameter relative to cell diameter
ratio of cell–cell to cell–medium surface tension
candidate_data: Published micropipette and contact-angle measurements of cell doublets, and microscopy images of cyanobacterial filaments from public image collections.

label: Tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120°, regardless of cell size
claim: In sections of tissues such as plant parenchyma, as in a froth of soap-bubbles, cell walls meet three at a time at angles of 120° whatever the sizes of the cells, while the relative sizes of neighbouring cells determine only the curvature of the walls.
quote: in both cases we see the cell-walls everywhere meeting, by threes, at angles of 120°, irrespective of the size of the individual cells: whose relative size, on the other hand, determines the _curvature_ of the partition-walls.
scope: plant parenchyma, honeycomb, segmenting eggs and other cellular complexes viewed perpendicular to the walls
measurable_quantities: number of walls meeting at each vertex
wall curvature versus size difference of neighbouring cells
candidate_data: Segmented epithelial and plant tissue images (e.g. Image Data Resource, published Drosophila wing-disc and plant meristem segmentations) from which vertex degree and junction angles can be measured.

label: Four cells of a segmenting egg never meet in a point; a polar furrow is always present
claim: In the four-celled stage of a segmenting egg whose cells are in full fluid contact, the four cells cannot meet in a single point; a short intermediate partition (the polar furrow) must be present, and reports of four cells meeting in a simple cross are due to error or imperfect observation.
quote: it is quite certain that no simple and homogeneous system of fluid films such as we are dealing with is in equilibrium without its presence.
scope: four-celled stage of segmenting eggs of animals in which blastomeres are in full fluid contact
measurable_quantities: presence and length of polar (cross) furrow
number of cells meeting at the animal and vegetal poles
candidate_data: Live-imaging and 3D segmentation datasets of early cleavage-stage embryos (e.g. published ascidian, sea urchin and frog embryo atlases) in which pole junction topology can be scored.

section: Unequal tensions and rounding of blastomeres
label: Strong cell–cell tension relative to cell–medium tension makes cells round off
claim: Where the tension at cell–cell contacts exceeds that at cell–medium surfaces, the external angle between neighbouring cells is less than 120°, and if the cell–cell tension equals or exceeds the sum of the other two the cells touch only at a point, which explains rounded-off blastomeres separated by spaces.
quote: If the former be greater than either of the other two, the outside angle will be less than 120°; and if the tension along the surface _cc′_ be as much or more than the sum of the other two, then the drops will stand in contact only, save for the possible effect of external pressure, at a point.
scope: blastomeres of segmenting eggs, pollen tetrads and filamentous algae in contact with a surrounding fluid
candidate_data: Published measurements of blastomere contact angles and cortical tension (micropipette aspiration) in early embryos, e.g. mouse and ascidian compaction studies.

section: Epidermal layer as a positional effect
label: An epidermis’s physical characters follow simply from its lying on the outside
claim: The fundamental character of an epidermis is that it lies on the outside of the cell mass, and its main physical features (flattened, rectangular cells meeting partitions at near right angles) follow from that position through unequal and consolidated tensions in its outer walls.
quote: the fundamental character of an epidermis simply is that it lies on the outside, and that its main physical characteristics follow, as a matter of course, from the position which it occupies and from the various consequences which that situation entails.
scope: epidermal tissue of plants (especially simple epidermal tissue as in Laminaria) and analogous outer cell layers
measurable_quantities: shape and aspect ratio of outer versus inner cells
angles at which anticlinal walls meet the outer wall
candidate_data: Segmented plant tissue sections and confocal stacks in public image repositories (e.g. Image Data Resource) comparing outer-layer and inner-layer cell geometry.

label: Cylinders or spheres pressed into full surface contact form hexagons
claim: Whenever cylinders or spheres of similar size are brought into complete surface contact by any uniform force (surface tension, growth pressure or external pressure), they tend to form a pattern of hexagons in section or surface view, each meeting six neighbours with 120° angles.
quote: wherever we have a system of cylinders or spheres, associated together with sufficient mutual interaction to bring them into complete surface contact, there, in section or in surface view, we tend to get a pattern of hexagons.
scope: epithelia, plant parenchyma, coral corallites, insect combs and other close-packed bodies of uniform size
candidate_data: Segmented epithelial images (e.g. Image Data Resource) giving polygon-number distributions, and coral specimen images in MorphoSource.

label: Hexagons are regular only where cells are equal in size and forces uniform
claim: Perfectly regular hexagonal cell patterns occur only where the cells are uniform in size and subject to uniform forces, as in the retinal pigment epithelium; where cell sizes vary (intestinal epithelium, parenchyma) or growth adds directional traction, the hexagons become irregular or elongated.
quote: the cells, uniform in size, are flattened out to a uniform thickness by the fluid pressure acting radially; and their reaction on each other converts the flattened discs into regular hexagons.
scope: animal epithelia (retinal pigment epithelium, intestinal and vascular epithelium) and plant epidermis
measurable_quantities: coefficient of variation of cell area
candidate_data: Published retinal pigment epithelium flat-mount morphometry datasets and segmented intestinal epithelium images in public repositories such as Image Data Resource.

label: Close-packed corallites of varying size are on average hexagonal
claim: In colonial corals whose corallites are in close contact, the corallites are squeezed into hexagonal prisms; where their sizes vary irregularly they are hexagonal on average, some having fewer and some more than six sides, while loosely bundled corallites stay cylindrical.
quote: where there is greater and more irregular variation in size, the cells will be _on the average_ hexagonal, but some will have fewer and some more sides than six
scope: massive versus fasciculate colonial corals (e.g. Lithostrotion, Cyathophyllum, Arachnophyllum)
candidate_data: Coral specimen images and 3D scans in MorphoSource and fossil occurrence and growth-form data in the Paleobiology Database.

label: The bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism capped by rhombic-dodecahedral facets
claim: The hive-bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism closed at one end by three rhombic facets of a rhombic dodecahedron meeting at about 109° 28′, the configuration that encloses a given volume with the least surface.
quote: The bee’s cell, then, is this figure incompletely formed: it is a hexagonal prism with one open or unfinished end, and one trihedral apex of a rhombic dodecahedron.
scope: comb cells of the hive-bee
measurable_quantities: rhomb angles at the base of the cell
wax surface area per unit cell volume
candidate_data: Published micro-CT studies of honeybee comb geometry and 3D scans of combs; no single standard repository known.

label: Comb geometry arises from surface tension in semi-fluid wax, not bee design
claim: The regular hexagonal and pyramidal geometry of the bee’s comb is produced automatically by surface tension acting on the cell walls while the wax (or the wasp’s paper pulp) is still semi-fluid, the insects merely building thin tubular cells packed closely together; it is not due to the bee seeking to economise wax.
quote: It seems more likely that we have to do with a true surface-tension effect; in other words, that the walls assume their configuration when in a semi-fluid state, while the papery pulp is still liquid, or while the wax is warm under the high temperature of the crowded hive
scope: comb-building social bees and wasps
measurable_quantities: cell shape at initial construction versus later
candidate_data: Published thermography and time-lapse studies of honeybee comb construction; no dedicated public database known.

label: Parenchyma cells are generally rhombic dodecahedra, ideal froths tetrakaidecahedra
claim: A perfectly fluid froth of equal cells is divided into Kelvin’s fourteen-sided tetrakaidecahedra, but in plant parenchyma, given restraint and imperfect fluidity, the cells generally take the rhombic dodecahedral form even under symmetrical conditions.
quote: Accordingly, it is very probably the case that, in the parenchymatous tissue, under the actual conditions of restraint and of very imperfect fluidity, it is after all the rhombic dodecahedral configuration which, even under perfectly symmetrical conditions, is generally assumed.
scope: isolated cells of symmetrical plant parenchyma of near-equal cell size
measurable_quantities: number of quadrilateral, pentagonal and hexagonal faces
candidate_data: 3D segmented plant tissue volumes from confocal or micro-CT imaging in public repositories (e.g. Image Data Resource), giving face counts per cell.

label: Physical laws govern the whole configuration of later-stage segmenting eggs
claim: The whole configuration of an egg in advanced stages of segmentation is determined by simple physical laws just as in the two- and four-celled stages, even though the mathematics becomes too difficult to follow.
quote: We have little reason to doubt, and no just cause to disbelieve, that the whole configuration, for instance of an egg in the advanced stages of segmentation, is accurately determined by simple physical laws
scope: segmenting eggs of animals at all cleavage stages
measurable_quantities: cell positions and shapes in embryos
agreement of physical foam or vertex models with observed embryo geometry
candidate_data: Published 3D cell-shape atlases of early embryos (e.g. C. elegans and ascidian embryo segmentations) compared against foam and vertex-model simulations.

section: Polar furrow variants and cell size
label: Polar-furrow arrangements follow relative cell sizes, not species identity
claim: Small changes in the relative sizes of the four cells carry the median partition and its polar furrows through all their possible arrangements, which correspond to those observed in various embryos; these arrangements are physical phenomena distributed without relation to zoological classification, not species characters.
quote: So, by slight and delicate modifications in the relative size of the cells, we may pass through all the possible arrangements of the median partition, and of the “furrows” which correspond to its upper and lower edges; and every one of these arrangements has been frequently observed in the four-celled stage of various embryos.
scope: four-celled stage of embryos across molluscs, annelids, coelenterates, vertebrates and others
measurable_quantities: upper and lower polar furrow lengths
candidate_data: Published blastomere volume and cleavage-geometry measurements from imaging studies of early spiralian, ascidian and frog embryos.

label: No evidence that physical forces give way to unknown vital agencies in development
claim: Although forces other than surface tension act in a growing embryo, there is no evidence at any stage that physical forces cease to govern its material form and are replaced by agencies unknown to physics.
quote: But we have no evidence whatsoever that at this point, or that point, or at any, the dominion of the physical forces over the material system gives place to a new condition where agencies at present unknown to the physicist impose themselves on the living matter
scope: developing embryos and living tissues generally
candidate_data: none known

label: Minimal bisecting walls cut the longest axis and alternate at right angles
claim: For a rectangular cell to be divided equally by a partition of least area, the partition must cut across its longest axis, and in successive bisections each new partition must be at right angles to the one before.
quote: From this we may draw the simple rule that, for a rectangular body or parallelopiped to be divided equally by means of a partition of minimal area, (1) the partition must cut across the longest axis of the figure; and (2) in the event of successive bisections, each partition must run at right angles to its immediate predecessor.
scope: dividing cells of roughly rectangular shape, especially in plant tissues
measurable_quantities: orientation of division plane relative to cell long axis
candidate_data: Time-lapse lineage-tracked plant meristem and early embryo datasets (e.g. published Arabidopsis embryo and shoot-apex segmentations) recording division-plane orientation.

section: Sachs’s and Errera’s rules of division
label: A new cell wall has the least area that can enclose the given volume (Errera)
claim: The fundamental rule of cell division is that the incipient partition of a dividing cell takes the least possible area that can divide the given volume; Sachs’s rule of successive divisions at right angles is a subordinate case of this principle.
quote: a much more important and fundamental rule, due not to Sachs but to Errera; that (3) the incipient partition-wall of a dividing cell tends to be such that its area is the least possible by which the given space-content can be enclosed.
scope: dividing cells, especially plant cells and blastomeres
measurable_quantities: area of alternative partitions dividing the same volume
candidate_data: Published 3D segmented plant embryo and meristem datasets in which observed division planes have been compared to computed minimal-area planes.

section: Unequal division of a cubical cell
label: A cell cutting off under ~3/10 of its volume uses a curved corner wall, not a plane
claim: When a cubical or rectangular cell divides unequally and the smaller part is less than about three-tenths of the whole, the minimal partition is a quarter-cylinder cutting off one corner rather than a plane wall; below about 0.15 of the volume a spherical octant in a corner is smaller still.
quote: that one portion by anything less than about three-tenths of the whole, or three-sevenths of the other portion, there will be a tendency for the cell to divide, not by means of a plane transverse partition, but by means of a curved, cylindrical wall cutting off one corner of the original cell
scope: unequally dividing rectangular plant cells, e.g. hairs in Fucus conceptacles, moss paraphyses, stomatal precursor cells
candidate_data: Imaging datasets of asymmetric divisions in plant epidermis (e.g. published stomatal lineage time-lapse studies) giving daughter volume ratios and wall shapes.

section: Division of a flattened quadrant cell
label: A quadrant-shaped flat cell divides by a curved anticlinal wall about 3:7 along its side
claim: A flattened cell shaped like a quadrant of a circle divides into equal halves by a circular-arc anticlinal wall meeting the side and periphery at right angles, cutting off about 55° 22′ of the arc and starting about three-tenths of the radius from the centre, since this is the shortest bisecting wall.
quote: Now we find that a flattened cell which is approximately a quadrant of a circle invariably divides after the manner of Fig. 145, C, that is to say, by an approximately circular, _anticlinal_ wall
scope: flattened discoid algae (e.g. Erythrotrichia) and eggs flattened under pressure (frog, sea-urchin) at the eight-cell stage
measurable_quantities: position of new wall on the radial side
candidate_data: Imaging of compressed early embryos and discoid algal thalli in published developmental studies; no dedicated database known.

label: Sector cells divide anticlinally only between 62½° and 90°, otherwise periclinally
claim: A sector-shaped (triangular) cell is likely to divide by an anticlinal wall only when its angle of arc lies between about 62½° and 90°; narrower, more tapering cells divide by a periclinal wall, which then has the smaller area.
quote: We see from this, then, that what we have called an anticlinal partition, as _MP_, is only likely to occur in a triangular or prismatic cell whose angle of arc lies between 90° and 62½°. In all narrower or more tapering cells, the periclinal partition will be of less area, and will therefore be more and more likely to occur.
scope: wedge-shaped cells in flattened discs, growing points and embryos of plants and flattened eggs
measurable_quantities: sector angle of the mother cell
orientation of the new partition (anticlinal or periclinal)
candidate_data: Lineage-tracked plant embryo and meristem segmentations (published Arabidopsis embryo atlases) in which mother-cell geometry and division orientation can be scored.

section: Uniform growth and unequal cell division
label: Uniform growth of a disc makes its daughter cells divide at different times
claim: Uniform, symmetrical growth of a flattened disc does not imply uniform growth of its cells: after a quadrant divides into triangular and quadrilateral halves, the triangular cell gains area faster and reaches division size first (at about 1.345 times the radius, against about 1.517 for the quadrilateral).
quote: For it shews us that a uniform and symmetrical growth of the organism (symmetrical, that is to say, under the limitations of a plane surface, or plane section) by no means involves a uniform or symmetrical growth of the individual cells, but may, under certain conditions, actually lead to inequality among these
scope: flattened discoid cell aggregates growing uniformly, such as Erythrotrichia
measurable_quantities: timing of division of sister cells
cell area growth rate by position
candidate_data: Time-lapse imaging of discoid algal or plant tissue growth with lineage tracking; no dedicated public dataset known.

section: Origin of an epidermis by minimal-area division
label: Successive minimal-area divisions leave quadrilateral cells forming an epidermis
claim: Successive minimal-area divisions of a disc soon leave only quadrilateral cells at the periphery, which divide radially, producing a superficial layer of parallel-sided cells (an epidermis) contrasting with the irregular cells beneath.
quote: we shall consequently have a superficial or peripheral layer of quadrilateral cells, with sides approximately parallel, that is to say what we are accustomed to call _an epidermis_.
scope: discoid and rounded embryonic structures of plants (moss embryos, algal discs, antheridia)
measurable_quantities: shape of peripheral versus interior cells
orientation of divisions in the outer layer
candidate_data: Published segmented plant embryo atlases (e.g. Arabidopsis early embryo 3D segmentations) giving protoderm formation and division orientations.

label: All surface groupings of eight cells belong to one of thirteen types
claim: Because n cells sharing a common outer boundary and meeting three at a time need n − 3 intermediate partitions, every possible grouping of eight cells all reaching the surface belongs to one of thirteen topological types, so all drawings of such eight-celled structures represent one of these types.
quote: all possible groupings or arrangements whatsoever of eight cells (where all take part in the _surface_ of the group, none being submerged or wholly enveloped by the rest) are referable to some one or other of _thirteen_ types or forms.
scope: eight-celled aggregates of plants and animals with all cells at the surface (segmenting eggs, apical cones, discs)
candidate_data: Segmented images of eight-cell embryos and plant tissues from published embryo atlases, scored for junction topology.

label: Most stable cell groupings spread contacts evenly; unstable ones concentrate them
claim: Among the possible arrangements of a small group of cells, the most stable (and therefore commonest) are those in which the cell-to-cell contacts are most evenly divided among the cells, and the least stable are those in which one cell has a predominant number of contacts.
quote: But it would appear that the most stable arrangements are those in which the total number of contacts is most evenly divided, and the least stable are those in which some one cell has, as in type _f_, a predominant number of contacts.
scope: small aggregates of cells or drops (segmenting eggs, oil-drop models)
candidate_data: Live-imaging datasets of early cleavage embryos and foam or emulsion experiments recording neighbour topology over time.

label: The arrangement of the first eight cells is not a constant character of a species
claim: A particular arrangement of cell partitions at the eight-celled stage is not a specific or constant character of an organism; within a single species such as the frog, several essentially different arrangements occur.
quote: is a particular arrangement of cell-partitions to be looked upon (as the published figures of the embryologist are apt to suggest) as a _specific character_, or at least a constant or normal character, of the particular organism? The answer to this question is a direct negative
scope: eight-celled stage of eggs, especially the animal pole of the frog’s egg
measurable_quantities: frequency of each eight-cell arrangement type within a species
candidate_data: Large samples of imaged Xenopus or other amphibian eight-cell embryos from published developmental imaging studies; Xenbase may hold relevant images.

label: Few partition patterns recur across organisms regardless of classification
claim: Because a closed surface divided into a small number of faces admits only a small number of arrangements, the same few configurations of cells (and of parts and organs) recur in all kinds of plants and animals with no relation to biological classification.
quote: This is the simple reason why we meet in such a case as we have been discussing (viz. the arrangement of a group or system of eight cells) with the same few types recurring again and again in all sorts of organisms, plants as well as animals, and with no relation to the lines of biological classification
scope: small cell groups and partitioned organs across plants and animals
measurable_quantities: frequency of each partition topology by taxon
candidate_data: Cleavage-pattern descriptions compiled across taxa from published embryological imaging, combined with phylogenies (e.g. Open Tree of Life) to test phylogenetic signal.

label: A coral fossula reflects space-partitioning, not higher bilateral organisation
claim: The asymmetrical chamber (fossula) of corals such as Heterophyllia and Zaphrentis arises as one of the possible arrangements of septa meeting three at a time, and gives no grounds for interpreting it as a sign of bilaterality or a higher grade of organisation.
quote: Where a single fossula occurs, we are usually told that it is a symptom of “bilaterality”; and this is in turn interpreted as an indication of a higher grade of organisation than is implied in the purely “radial symmetry” of the commoner types of coral. The mathematical aspect of the case gives no warrant for this interpretation.
scope: rugose and other corals with septa meeting one another (Heterophyllia, Zaphrentis and allies)
candidate_data: Fossil coral specimen images in MorphoSource and occurrence and taxonomy data in the Paleobiology Database.

label: Stomata lie in rows on oblong-celled leaves and scattered on polygonal-celled ones
claim: Because the stomatal mother cell is cut off by a minimal partition whose form depends on epidermal cell shape, stomata are arranged in regular rows where epidermal cells are oblong (as in hyacinth) and irregularly where they are polygonal (as in Sedum).
quote: It is obvious that in the case of the oblong cells of the epidermis in the hyacinth the stomata will be found arranged in regular rows, while they will be irregularly distributed over the surface of the leaf in such a case as we have depicted in Sedum.
scope: leaf epidermis of monocotyledons with oblong cells and dicotyledons with polygonal cells
measurable_quantities: spatial arrangement of stomata (row alignment index)
candidate_data: Leaf epidermis micrograph collections and stomatal trait datasets (e.g. TRY plant traits for stomatal density, published leaf-epidermis image datasets).

label: Pollen-grain shape depends on whether walls harden before the tetrad separates
claim: Pollen grains and spores formed as tetrahedral tetrads keep the plane facets and sharp angles of the tetrad if their walls solidify before the grains separate, but become spherical if they separate while still soft.
quote: the pollen-grains afterwards fall apart, and their individual form will depend upon whether or no their walls have solidified before this liberation takes place.
scope: pollen grains of angiosperms and spores of ferns and red algae formed in tetrads
measurable_quantities: timing of wall hardening relative to tetrad separation
candidate_data: Palynological image databases (e.g. PalDat) of pollen morphology combined with developmental studies of tetrad separation timing.

label: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass
claim: The form of a growing organism regulates the form and number of the cells that compose it: the cell network is the result, not the cause, of the overall configuration, which is caused by whatever processes make growth faster in one direction than another.
quote: The complex cell-network is not the cause but the result of the general configuration, which latter has its essential cause in whatsoever physical and chemical processes have led to a varying velocity of growth in one direction as compared with another.
scope: growing multicellular plant and animal structures
candidate_data: Published time-lapse growth-tracking datasets of plant organs and mutants with altered cell division but normal shape (e.g. lineage-tracked shoot apex and leaf datasets).

section: Growth rate and plane of division
label: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency
claim: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.
quote: the manner in which this latter cell divides will simply depend upon the form it has assumed before each successive act of division takes place, that is to say upon the ratio between its rate of growth and the frequency of its successive divisions.
scope: apical and growing cells of mosses, liverworts, ferns and algae
candidate_data: Time-lapse imaging of moss protonemata and apical cells (e.g. published Physcomitrium growth studies) giving growth rates and division planes.

label: Outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells
claim: Because quadrangular cells subdivide by periclinal walls that strengthen the boundary while triangular cells divide by oblique anticlines, outward growth is greater over triangular cells, so buds and outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells, as is widely seen in cryptogams.
quote: As a direct and immediate consequence of this we might expect a tendency for special outgrowths, or “buds,” to arise from the triangular rather than from the quadrangular cells; and this turns out to be not merely a tendency towards which theoretical considerations point, but a widespread and important factor in the morphology of the cryptogams.
scope: growing points and buds of cryptogams (mosses, liverworts, ferns, algae)
measurable_quantities: shape of cells giving rise to buds
frequency of bud initiation by cell shape
candidate_data: Published lineage studies of bud and branch initiation in moss protonemata and fern gametophytes; no dedicated database known.
